text:
So what actually protected European investors? Three things, and none of them is a clever ETF.

First, owning something that isn't stocks. Here's a real sixty forty portfolio with euro government bonds, rebalanced every year, from the end of 1999.

At the end of 2002 it was down twenty-one percent instead of forty-five. It was back above ten thousand euros in 2005. Eight years earlier.

Even eighty twenty helped: the worst fall dropped from forty-seven to thirty-four percent.

But look at the recovery. The eighty twenty was only back above ten thousand euros in 2012, one year before all stocks. A small bond slice softens the fall. It takes a bigger one to shorten the wait.

The price? Today the sixty forty is worth about thirty-eight thousand six hundred, the eighty twenty forty-three thousand, against forty-six thousand for all stocks.

There's a hidden engine in there: rebalancing. At the end of 2002 and 2008, it forced you to sell bonds and buy cheap stocks. Exactly when nobody wanted to.

But there's a warning label. In 2022, euro government bonds lost about eighteen percent, the same year stocks fell.

Bonds protected you when interest rates fell. They don't when inflation and rates are rising. And euro area inflation is back at three point three percent, with the E C B raising rates to two and a half.

Second, matching your money to your time horizon. The world index needed thirteen years to recover from the dot-com top.

Picture someone who's fifty-eight and plans to retire at sixty-five. A thirteen year recovery takes them to seventy-one.

Money you need in the next five years has no business being one hundred percent in stocks. And a few months of expenses in cash means a broken car never forces you to sell at minus forty percent.

Just don't confuse safety with growth. Ten thousand euros at the E C B overnight rate from 2001 to 2025 became about fourteen thousand, and still lost around seventeen percent of its value to inflation.

If you're close to retirement, the order of returns matters even more. I covered that in my video on ten thousand European retirements.

Third, keep buying, and never sell in a panic. That's the one that mattered most.

Let's meet two investors. Both put ten thousand euros into world stocks at the end of 1999.

At the end of 2002, with forty-five percent gone, investor A panics. Sells everything, and puts the five thousand five hundred left into a savings account at two percent a year.

Investor B does nothing. Doesn't sell, doesn't check the app. Just waits.

Today, investor A has about eight thousand eight hundred euros. Less than they started with, almost twenty-seven years later.

Investor B has forty-six thousand.

Thirty-seven thousand euros. Same money, same index, same start date, same crash. One decision.

But maybe investor A was smarter than that. Maybe they bought back in once things calmed down.

Sell at the end of 2002, buy back at the end of 2006 when the recovery looked safe: thirty-one thousand four hundred.

Wait for the full recovery and buy back at the end of 2013: twenty-nine thousand four hundred.

Hold through the first crash, give up in 2008, come back in 2013: twenty-five thousand two hundred.

Every version of panic, even the clever ones, cost more than any crash scenario in this video.

And here's the cruel part. Investor A didn't feel stupid in 2003. They felt smart. Every bad headline for the next ten years told them they were right.

That's not just my replay. Morningstar's yearly Mind the Gap study keeps finding the same thing: investors earn less than the funds they own, because they buy after rises and sell after falls.
